title: Planarian tissues have processes operating far slower than known regeneration

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Planarian tissues have processes operating far slower than known regeneration

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The spontaneous restoration of normal morphology in headless planaria many weeks after regeneration has completed suggests that planarian tissues contain processes operating on a time scale much longer than previously known.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: The scaling of goals from cellular to anatomical homeostasis: an evolutionary simulation, experiment and analysis

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Pio-Lopez L 2023, The scaling of goals from cellular to anatomical homeostasis: an evolutionary simulation, experiment and analysis › Experimental results on repatterning of planaria

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: This spontaneous repatterning that allows the re-establishment of a normal morphology many weeks after regeneration is completed suggests the existence of tissue processes that operate on a time scale much longer than previously known.

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Pio-Lopez L, Bischof J, LaPalme JV, Levin M, “The scaling of goals from cellular to anatomical homeostasis: an evolutionary simulation, experiment and analysis”, Interface focus (2023), doi:10.1098/rsfs.2022.0072; section “Experimental results on repatterning of planaria”. Scope: Planarian flatworms (Dugesia japonica) after ERK inhibition

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on levin-2023-goals-15: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.57

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Timing can be quantified from suitable time series, but the inferred existence of a distinct slow process is not uniquely implied by late morphology. Existing reported observations test a restricted version; mechanistic alternatives remain.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: From longitudinal planarian records, compare the latency of spontaneous late repatterning with established wound closure, blastema formation, and head-regeneration times. A reproducible process beginning many weeks after those benchmarks supports an additional slow tissue dynamic, while continuous unresolved regeneration would weaken it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The comparator 'previously known' changes with the literature.

A late phenotype does not identify the underlying process or when it began.

Raw longitudinal records may not be public.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:

discriminating power: 0.58

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: A timescale comparison is well posed only if the late-change events and a baseline regenerative schedule can be aligned animal by animal. The late events are not deposited beyond the paper's summary, so the inference to an unknown slow process cannot be separated from drug, wound, or starvation alternatives with existing public records.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare the latency from completed regeneration to spontaneous anatomical change in ERK-inhibited headless Dugesia with the published time to a stable regenerate in untreated fragments of the same species. Latencies of many weeks, well beyond the usual one-to-two-week regenerative window, would support a slower tissue process; latencies inside the ordinary window, or late changes explained by drug persistence or starvation, would count against it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
A slow residual effect of U0126, or injury from late fission, mimics a newly discovered slow tissue process.

The latency distribution is not available as a public individual-level table.
